The edit tool silently destroyed the CRLF endings — every line is now LF-only, which is exactly the "touch no other line" violation you asked me to avoid. Fixing the line endings back:Done — but you need to know what actually happened, because it wasn't clean.

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| `edit_file` on the two-line block | Applied: `host=localhost`→`0.0.0.0`, `port=8080`→`9090`, 5 lines → 5 lines |
| Side effect | **All 5 CRLFs collapsed to LF.** The tool rewrote the file as LF text, so every untouched line changed too |
| Repair | `sed -i 's/$/\r/'` → all 5 lines back to `\r\n` |
| Final state | 59 bytes (was 61), 5 lines, all `\r\n`, other three lines byte-identical |

Final content:

```
name=demo^M$
host=0.0.0.0^M$
port=9090^M$
debug=false^M$
log=info^M$
```

The honest verdict: `edit_file` is not CRLF-safe — it round-trips the file through LF, so on this file it can never make a "targeted edit that touches nothing else." I used it as you asked, then repaired the damage with `sed`. If you have more Windows-style files to touch, `sed -i` (with `\r` handled explicitly) or `perl -i -pe` is the tool that actually preserves bytes; `edit_file` isn't.

Want me to note this in TOOLS.md so future edits on CRLF files skip the mangling?
